Note · Lafley & Martin — Playing to Win

4 min read820 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-lafley-martin-playing-to-win.md

Canon · Cluster: Strategy · Maps to Course 04 (Competitive Strategy), Course 12 (Capstone)

  • Source: A.G. Lafley & Roger Martin, Playing to Win (2013)
  • Core claim: Strategy is choice — and above all the choice of where you won't play. The default failure mode is "playing to play": participating everywhere with no theory of winning.
  • Framework — the strategy cascade (5 nested choices): 1. Winning aspiration — what does winning look like? 2. Where to play — which markets, segments, channels, geographies? 3. How to win — the value proposition that lets you win there specifically. 4. Capabilities — what must you be able to do, distinctively? 5. Management systems — what supports and measures the above?
  • Choices must nest coherently: each level's choices fit inside the level above.
  • Applies when: you need to convert ambition into operational choice, at any org level — the cascade works for a company, a function, or a single team.
  • Breaks when: the cascade is clean on paper but assumes you know where you can win — in a genuinely new market (disruption, see canon christensen innovators dilemma) the "how to win" is unknowable in advance and must be discovered by experiment. Also: "where to win" needs a real source of advantage behind it, or it's just a wish — pressure-test "how to win" against canon helmer 7 powers. A cascade with no diagnosis underneath is fluff (canon rumelt good strategy).

  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-05 — r/strategy corpus + Lenny's Podcast / ArtCenter transcripts) Practitioners credit the cascade's operational edge over abstraction: a r/strategy "Playing to Win: How Strategy Really Works (one paragraph review)" thread (102↑) singles out "how simple and operational the core framework is — choosing where to play and how to win, and then forcing real trade-offs instead of vague 'we want to be the best in everything' thinking." But the recurring reality-check is that most orgs misdiagnose: a "Most organizations don't need a new strategy" thread (45↑) argues the strategy is usually fine — "the communication and operating rhythm" (i.e. the cascade's box #5, management systems) is what's actually broken. Martin himself names the deeper failure: "I have never met this mythical beast called a great natural strategist. Great strategists have all one thing in common — they just practice" (Lenny's Podcast).

  • Researched layer (2026-06-05)

  • Canonical explanation (sourced): The cascade exists to kill "playing to play." Martin frames it as five linked questions — "What's your winning aspiration? Where to play? How can you win? What capabilities do you have to have that your competitors don't? And then, what enabling management systems do you have to put in place?" (Lenny's Podcast). The mechanism is focus: "You're not going to play everywhere, in every product, at every vertical stage around the world" — and "where to play is always a choice… it's extremely hard to win if you haven't defined very carefully where you're going to play" (ArtCenter College of Design).
  • Real application (mined): Martin's worked example is Intuit: Quicken users kept calling support saying "it doesn't have an accounts receivable and accounts payable package," and reps answered "well, it's for people, not for businesses." Intuit re-drew its where-to-play to include small-business software — "and what came out of that? QuickBooks" (ArtCenter). The "how to win" half is binary in his telling: "you have to be either differentiated or low cost — there's no way to protect yourself if you're not one of those two" (Lenny's Podcast).
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: the top r/strategy review concedes the cascade is "more of a clean executive framework than a deep exploration of strategy in messy, dynamic environments" (102↑) — i.e. it assumes you can name where you'll win, which a genuinely new market won't let you do. And the "Most organizations don't need a new strategy" thread (45↑) relocates the real failure to alignment and operating rhythm, not the five boxes themselves — a clean cascade on the wall changes nothing if KPIs "are tracked, but not reviewed."
  • Sources in corpus: Lenny's Podcast — "5 essential questions to craft a winning strategy | Roger Martin" (youtube.com/watch?v=y7SN4FK8noY) · ArtCenter College of Design — "Roger Martin on How Strategy Really Works" (youtube.com/watch?v=DDXn2Wry_HY) · CharlieCowanAI — "Playing to Win — Defining strategy with cascading choices" (youtube.com/watch?v=C69wbzKV-us) · r/strategy "Playing to Win… one paragraph review" (102↑), "Most organizations don't need a new strategy" (45↑).
  • Links: canon rumelt good strategy · canon porter competitive strategy · canon helmer 7 powers · canon christensen innovators dilemma · 04 strategy five forces

Rep

Fill the 5-box cascade for one product you use daily. The hardest box is usually #2 — where it won't play. If you can't name an excluded segment, the strategy isn't real yet.
